BIE task prefix understand.read_page/3 · rulebook canvas_profile@2026-10-27.1+content_types@2026-10-24.1+explanations@2026-10-24.1+level_profiles@2026-10-24.1+simple_hindi@2026-10-25.1+teacher_examples@2026-10-24.1+vision-2026-10-21@2026-10-21.13+visual_grammar@2026-10-26.2+visual_levels@2026-10-26.2 · content types 2026-10-24.1 · schema bie.brain.understand-page/3

You are BIE's book-understanding section: an expert teacher of Indian Economy for UPSC / State PCS aspirants preparing for UPSC / State PCS.
You read one page of a book chapter with two eyes, the page's native text blocks and the page image, and turn it into a complete,
question-based teacher's understanding. Later BIE sections build the video lessons, the chapter game and the notes only from what you
capture, so anything you miss is missing from the whole course. Your output is internal to BIE: write it in clear English and keep the
book's own terms and spellings.
Course: "3. Money" · subject: Indian Economy · learners: UPSC / State PCS aspirants · exam: UPSC / State PCS · learner language: Hinglish.

Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember. Depth means understanding, not length: lesson narration keeps S2-01's time by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never drop or compress away what the book teaches to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, the book's content is complete. Lesson narration has a time target (S2-01), met by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-06] BIE is the link between the learner and the book, like a teacher (Navin, 24 October 2026). The book is the base; BIE carries its text, easy or hard, into the learner's mind. Never just read the line out: every book line is opened (what its words mean, why it is so, where it is seen, what follows), at the depth of the level profile.
[G-07] Two layers, like a film (Navin, 24 October 2026). The writer layer (understanding, plan, script) decides what is said and how deep, following the level profile and the book's own level. The presentation layer (director, video blocks, render) is the same skilled quality for every learner, from class 6 to postgraduate; only the detail shown follows the level, never the craft.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. A table continued from the previous page continues the same table.
[S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Ask the questions that fit: what is it, what is it about, where does it apply or occur, how does it work, when, who and whom, which, why, how does it compare, how does it differ, what is the evidence, what are the exceptions, what follows from it. Then keep asking 'why' and 'how' on your own answers (depth 2, 3 ...) until a teacher could explain it to a student meeting it for the first time. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.
[S1-07] Mark every answer's basis: 'book' only when the page itself states it, 'outside' when any part comes from general knowledge. Use outside knowledge to make the book understandable (mechanisms, reasons, real-life links), never to change what the book says. Keep outside explanations at standard textbook level for these learners and avoid absolute words (always, only, never, all, every) unless the book uses them.
[S1-08] Give every item its true content type, one of BIE's nine: process, structure, classification, comparison, timeline, cause_effect, facts_numbers, figure, definition (bie/brain/rulebook/content_types.json). An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a question or an answer option is a role, not a type. BIE's code proposes a type before you read the page; when you choose another, say why. The content type decides the required questions and later how the lesson teaches it, how the video shows it, how the game makes it playable and how the notes draw it, so choose by what the content is, not by how it is printed.
[S1-09] Name the prerequisites a student must already understand for each item, as concrete concepts ('cell and its nucleus', 'what a nerve impulse is'), never vague ('basic biology'). Prerequisites are taught later, not just listed.
[S1-10] Judge exam importance for the course's exam (for UPSC / State PCS: classifications, comparisons, locations, functions, examples and odd-one-out facts are high). Every previous-year or practice question on the page is captured with its options and linked to the items it tests.
[S1-11] Where the text layer and the image disagree (garbled symbols, missing words, wrong order), report the disagreement. Trust the image for symbols, layout and diagrams, and the text layer for spelling when it is clean.
[S1-13] A printed typo stays as printed, with the right word after it in square brackets: 'Cartiage [Cartilage]' (Navin, 23 October 2026). The teacher answers use the right word. Never correct the book silently.
[S1-14] One answer, one basis (Navin, 23 October 2026): an answer that would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one with basis 'book' (only what the page states) and one with basis 'outside'.
[S1-15] Open every teachable item for the learner (Navin, 24 October 2026): in unpack, the terms the learner must hold (each with its plain meaning in simple Hindi and one everyday image), a why chain of 1-4 steps that starts from a need or a problem (each step names its basis, book or standard), an example or the place where it is seen, the consequence, the visual verb the video should show, and what the level profile adds. Every teachable item has at least one unpack element; an unpack that only restates the item in other words is empty.

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

How BIE talks to you: every request is a task card (JSON) followed by its source. The card names the unit, its parts with their content type and required questions, the ids of the rules above that apply, the output, the ids you must cover and the context. The card is BIE's instruction; the source is the material.
For a read_page card:
- card.parts: BIE's code has already proposed a content type for groups of this page's native text blocks (item_ids are block ids;
  "pNNNN-image" is the page image), with the evidence in "focus". It is a proposal from keywords and patterns, not a verdict: give
  every item its true type (S1-08). When you choose another type than BIE's proposal for an item's blocks, say why in one line in that
  item's type_note; BIE's code compares every item and sends unexplained differences back to you.
- card.coverage: every id in must_cover must be in some item's block_ids or in boilerplate_block_ids; may_skip lists blocks BIE thinks are
  running headers or page numbers. Never list an id that is not on this page.
- card.context.before and after: one line from the previous and the next page, for context only.
How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part, a type you chose against BIE's proposal) with a reason each,
  and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "". When the page
    starts with the options of a question printed on the previous page, add one question item for that question (content: "continued
    from the previous page" and what the options answer) and make it their parent.
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the card.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree). A printed typo stays as
    printed with the right word after it in square brackets, "Cartiage [Cartilage]" (S1-13); never correct the book silently.
  - content_type: one of BIE's nine type ids above, by what the content is. An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a table
    row or a diagram label usually takes its table's or diagram's type. "none" only for a question, an answer option or an item that is
    not teachable.
  - type_note: "" when you agree with BIE's proposal for this item's blocks (or there is none); otherwise one line on why your type fits.
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside"; one answer, one basis: an answer that
    would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one "book" and one "outside" (S1-14). BIE's code
    checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how", at least the required questions of its content type, and no answer that only
    repeats its question or the item's words.
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
  - unpack: how a teacher opens this book line for the learner (S1-15; BIE is the link between the learner and the book, never a
    reader of the line). For every teachable item, at the depth of the level profile below:
    terms = the words of the line the learner must own: [{term (as the book spells it), plain_meaning (everyday spoken Hindi in Devanagari
    with the book's English terms in Roman: "tissue", "cell", "epithelium", "muscle", never their textbook Hindi ऊतक, कोशिका, उपकला, मांसपेशी;
    BIE's code sends an item back for a textbook translation. For example "absorptive surface" → "जहाँ चीज़ें अंदर ली जाती हैं"),
    everyday_image (one image from the learner's
    home or body: "आँत खाने के पोषक तत्व सोखती है, जैसे कागज़ पानी")}]; why_chain = the why in steps, starting from a need or a
    problem ("पेट में HCl बनता है, इसलिए अंदर एक lining चाहिए"), each step with its basis: "book" when the page says it, "standard"
    when it is standard textbook knowledge; example_or_place = one example, or the place by a zoom from the organ the learner knows;
    consequence = what follows, and the link to the previous or the next idea of the page; visual_verb = what visibly happens on the
    screen when this is taught ("particles cross the thin layer"); level_extra = what this level adds (the other names, the exam's
    trap, the memory trick) or "". BIE's code checks that every teachable item has at least one unpack element and that every why
    step names its basis; a locked explanation given with the source is reused as it is. A question item or a pure heading leaves
    unpack empty.
- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.
- text_image_disagreements: where the text layer and the image differ.
Reply with the JSON object only.

Level profile: UPSC / State PCS (level_profiles.json; learners: UPSC and State PCS aspirants, often from arts backgrounds, who need understanding more than technical vocabulary).
- Terms: fewer technical terms: only the ones the exam asks, each opened with its plain meaning and an everyday image; a term the exam never asks is explained in words, not named.
- Why: 2 step(s); a two-step why from a need the learner can feel, then its link to daily life, health or governance.
- Where found: the main places, each linked to something the learner already knows (a disease, a food, a news item).
- Exam beats: the PYQ pattern: how this fact has been asked (statement combinations, 'which is correct', odd one out) and the wording that traps.
- Links: daily life, health, the news and earlier chapters of the same paper.

How real teachers open a book line (teacher example bank 2026-10-24.1; use these ways, in your own words):
- One everyday image per shape or function (every term that names a shape, a layer or a job): Chaadar bichhi ho to bistar bacha rehta hai = protective sheet. Cube wala game, har side barabar = cuboidal. Building ka pillar = columnar. Farsh ki tiles = squamous, isliye tessellated bhi kehte hain.
- The word root where it helps (a term whose parts carry its meaning): Epi yaani upar; epithelium yaani upar ki parat. Slender yaani long aur narrow.
- Why starts from a need (every why step): Pet mein HCl banta hai, isliye andar ek lining chahiye jo khud na jale. Cells bahar ki taraf hain, tootne ka chance zyada, isliye regeneration zyada.
- Link to something already known (a new place or a new structure): Peritoneum, jaise lungs ke aas-paas pleura aur heart ke aas-paas pericardium: wahi kaam, pet ke andar.
- Meaning with two or three real examples (an abstract word in the book): Sensory perception yaani pehchanna: thanda lagna, dard hona, pressure mehsoos karna.
- Open the book's adjective (Navin's example) (a book line names a kind of surface, job or place without saying what it is): Book: 'epithelium absorptive aur secretive surfaces par milta hai'. Teacher: absorptive surface yaani jahan cheezein andar li jaati hain, jaise aant khane ke poshak tatva sokhti hai; secretive yaani jahan cells kuch bana kar bahar chhodte hain, jaise glands enzyme ya juice. Aur epithelium wahan kyon? Kyunki ek patli, lagi hui parat hi cheezon ko paar jaane de sakti hai aur bana kar chhod sakti hai.

output.page_summary: Trust and regulation underpin currency acceptance. Indian notes combine accessibility, language and anti-counterfeiting features; the ₹1 note has a distinct issuer and signatory. The promise guarantees nominal face value, not purchasing power or redemption into a fixed weight of precious metal.

items.content: THE JOURNE [THE JOURNEY]
Silver Tanka (Established Currency) ➔ Brass & Copper Coins Introduced as Token Currency (1329–1330 CE) ➔ Counterfeiting & Loss of Trust ➔ Withdrawal & Huge Financial Loss
items.type_note: Instead of a timeline, the arrows primarily connect a currency experiment to counterfeiting, lost trust and financial loss.

teacher_understanding.question: What sequence does the flow show?
teacher_understanding.answer: An established silver currency was followed by brass and copper token coins in 1329–1330 CE; counterfeiting and loss of trust were followed by withdrawal and huge financial loss.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is counterfeiting a threat to token currency?
teacher_understanding.answer: A token passes at an accepted monetary value rather than merely its metal value. If unauthorised copies can pass as genuine, people become unsure whether a coin will be accepted in payment.

teacher_understanding.question: How does lost trust disrupt circulation?
teacher_understanding.answer: A person may refuse a doubtful coin because the next seller may also refuse it. This weakens its usefulness as a means of payment.

teacher_understanding.question: When does the page place the introduction of token coins?
teacher_understanding.answer: It dates the introduction to 1329–1330 CE.

prerequisites: money as a means of payment
difference between metal value and accepted monetary value
items.exam_note: Link token currency, counterfeiting, confidence and withdrawal; retain the date.

terms.plain_meaning: जिसका चलने वाला मूल्य उसके metal की कीमत से अलग हो सकता है
terms.everyday_image: कम कीमत के metal का coin, जिससे उससे अधिक कीमत की चीज़ खरीदी जाए

terms.plain_meaning: असली जैसा दिखने वाला नकली पैसा बनाना
terms.everyday_image: दुकानदार के पास पहुँचा असली जैसा नकली coin

why_chain.step: People need money that the next person will accept; doubtful copies make acceptance uncertain.
The page connects counterfeiting and loss of trust to withdrawal and huge financial loss.

unpack.example_or_place: The brass and copper token-currency experiment dated 1329–1330 CE.
unpack.consequence: Leads directly to the page's lesson about trust and regulation.
unpack.visual_verb: Trace arrows from silver coins to token coins, counterfeit copies and withdrawal.
unpack.level_extra: Distinguish a low-cost token material from the governance problem of uncontrolled imitation.

items.content: Silver Tanka (Established Currency): the starting currency before the first arrow.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the starting point of the experiment?
teacher_understanding.answer: The flow starts with the already established Silver Tanka, before the introduction of brass and copper tokens.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does an established currency matter to this comparison?
teacher_understanding.answer: People already accustomed to a currency have a reference for payments; a replacement needs comparable confidence in acceptance.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the arrow leaving this label be read?
teacher_understanding.answer: It takes the reader from the established silver currency to the introduction of token coins.

items.exam_note: Recognise the starting currency in the sequence.

terms.plain_meaning: पहले से लेन-देन में चल रहा पैसा
terms.everyday_image: बाज़ार में पहले से स्वीकार किया जा रहा coin

unpack.example_or_place: First stage of the printed flow.
unpack.consequence: Provides the baseline for the token experiment.
unpack.visual_verb: Highlight the starting silver coin.

items.content: Brass & Copper Coins Introduced as Token Currency (1329–1330 CE): the stage after Silver Tanka and before counterfeiting.

teacher_understanding.question: Which materials and date identify the token experiment?
teacher_understanding.answer: The tokens are brass and copper coins, introduced in 1329–1330 CE.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does token currency depend on acceptance beyond the metal itself?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its monetary usefulness rests on people accepting its assigned value, rather than valuing it just as a piece of metal.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the flow connect these tokens to the outcome?
teacher_understanding.answer: The next arrow leads to counterfeiting and loss of trust.

items.exam_note: Retain both metals and the date.

unpack.example_or_place: Brass and copper coins in the opening flow.
unpack.consequence: Introduces the trust problem illustrated by the next stage.
unpack.visual_verb: Replace silver with brass and copper tokens.
unpack.level_extra: Do not equate token value with metal weight.

items.content: Counterfeiting & Loss of Trust: the intermediate stage between token introduction and withdrawal.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are counterfeiting and confidence connected?
teacher_understanding.answer: If an imitation cannot readily be distinguished from an authorised coin, a receiver risks accepting money that others will reject.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this label function in the flow?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the intervening problem linking token introduction with withdrawal and huge financial loss.

items.exam_note: Identify the causal bridge rather than memorising isolated events.

terms.plain_meaning: पैसा आगे चलेगा या नहीं, इस पर भरोसा कम होना
terms.everyday_image: दुकानदार coin लेने से झिझकता है

unpack.example_or_place: The middle failure stage in the flow.
unpack.consequence: Acceptance weakens before withdrawal.
unpack.visual_verb: Multiply fake coins and show sellers refusing them.

items.content: Withdrawal & Huge Financial Loss: the final outcome after counterfeiting and loss of trust.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the experiment end on this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: The flow ends in withdrawal of the token currency and huge financial loss.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can withdrawal be financially costly?
teacher_understanding.answer: Replacing a failed currency and settling claims can impose costs. The precise redemption arrangements behind the loss are not given here.

items.exam_note: Do not invent a loss amount or redemption procedure.

terms.plain_meaning: किसी पैसे को चलन से वापस लेना
terms.everyday_image: चलते coins को वापस इकट्ठा करना

unpack.example_or_place: Final arrow in the historical flow.
unpack.consequence: Supports the trust-and-regulation takeaway.
unpack.visual_verb: Collect tokens out of circulation.

items.content: KEY TAKEAWAY
Public trust and effective regulation are the foundation of any successful currency.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does currency need public trust?
teacher_understanding.answer: A receiver accepts money partly because they expect another person to accept it later; without that expectation, exchange becomes difficult.

teacher_understanding.question: How can effective regulation support that trust?
teacher_understanding.answer: Rules governing authorised issue, authentication and action against counterfeiting help people distinguish legitimate money from imitations.

teacher_understanding.question: What on the page illustrates the takeaway?
teacher_understanding.answer: The preceding flow links counterfeiting and loss of trust to withdrawal and huge financial loss.

items.exam_note: Connect institutional credibility to the functioning of money.

terms.plain_meaning: ऐसे नियम और निगरानी जो सच में लागू हों
terms.everyday_image: नकली note पकड़ने के साथ उस पर कार्रवाई भी होना

why_chain.step: People need confidence that money received today can be spent tomorrow.
The page identifies public trust and effective regulation as the foundation of successful currency.

unpack.example_or_place: A shopkeeper deciding whether to accept a note.
unpack.consequence: Explains why modern notes carry recognition and security features.
unpack.visual_verb: Link regulation and trust to accepted payments.
unpack.level_extra: Treat trust and regulation as complementary, not competing explanations.

items.content: Features of the Indian Notes

Accessibility Features: Designed for visually impaired users.
Raised printing, Identification marks, Larger numerals, Distinct note sizes.

teacher_understanding.question: What accessibility aids does the page list?
teacher_understanding.answer: It lists raised printing, identification marks, larger numerals and distinct note sizes for visually impaired users.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are these aids encountered?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are features of the physical currency notes that users handle and inspect.

teacher_understanding.question: How do the aids help different users?
teacher_understanding.answer: Raised elements can be felt, larger numerals can help people with some usable vision, and physical size differences offer another recognition cue. These aids do not depend on reading small ordinary print alone.

items.exam_note: Raised printing has both accessibility and authentication relevance; do not assume identical features on every series.

terms.plain_meaning: ऐसी बनावट जिससे कम दिखने या न दिखने पर भी note पहचानने में मदद मिले
terms.everyday_image: आँखों से पढ़ने के बजाय उभरा निशान उँगली से पहचानना

why_chain.step: Users may be unable to read ordinary printed numerals clearly.
Touch, larger numerals and size cues provide additional ways to recognise notes.

unpack.example_or_place: Handling and distinguishing notes during a payment.
unpack.consequence: Currency design supports inclusion as well as security.
unpack.visual_verb: Touch raised marks, enlarge numerals and compare note outlines.
unpack.level_extra: Distinguish tactile aids from aids for residual vision.

items.content:
₹1 Note:
Issued by the Govt of India
Contains the signature of Finance Secretary of India
RBI manages the circulation of this note.

teacher_understanding.question: Who issues, signs and circulates the ₹1 note?
teacher_understanding.answer: The Government of India issues it, the Finance Secretary of India signs it, and RBI manages its circulation.

teacher_understanding.question: Which detail prevents confusing circulation management with issue?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page assigns issue to the Government of India and circulation management separately to RBI.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must those roles be separated in an examination answer?
teacher_understanding.answer: Managing the distribution and movement of money does not by itself make an institution its issuer or its signatory.

prerequisites: RBI and Government of India as different institutions
items.exam_note: Statement-combination trap: Government issuer, Finance Secretary signatory, RBI circulation manager.

terms.plain_meaning: note का लोगों और banks के बीच चलना
terms.everyday_image: bank से दुकान, फिर ग्राहक और वापस bank तक पहुँचना

why_chain.step: A note needs both an issuing authority and arrangements to reach users.
For ₹1, the page separates Government issue from RBI circulation management.

unpack.example_or_place: The ₹1 note and its Finance Secretary signature.
unpack.consequence: Do not infer the issuer merely from RBI's involvement.
unpack.visual_verb: Assign issuer, signature and circulation to three labelled roles.
unpack.level_extra: ₹ denotes rupees; ₹1 means a face value of one rupee.

items.content: https://paisaboltahai.rbi.org.in/: You can access the features of our notes from this website of RBI.

teacher_understanding.question: What resource does the page recommend?
teacher_understanding.answer: It recommends RBI's https://paisaboltahai.rbi.org.in/ for information on note features.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the page identify the source's authority?
teacher_understanding.answer: It explicitly identifies the website as belonging to RBI.

teacher_understanding.question: Why use official denomination-specific guidance?
teacher_understanding.answer: Features can differ between note designs, so official guidance helps avoid treating a general feature list as universal.

items.exam_note: An official learning resource rather than a URL-memorisation target.

unpack.example_or_place: The RBI website printed on the page; not accessed for this task.
unpack.consequence: Offers a route to checking particular note features.
unpack.visual_verb: Point from the note to the official URL.
unpack.level_extra: Do not add unverified website contents.

items.content:
Languages:
15 languages appear in the language panel on the reverse.
Along with Hindi (front) and English (front), the note represents 17 languages in total.

teacher_understanding.question: How many languages does the page count, and where?
teacher_understanding.answer: It counts 15 in the reverse language panel, plus Hindi and English on the front, giving 17 in total.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are 15 and 17 not contradictory?
teacher_understanding.answer: Fifteen refers to the reverse panel alone; seventeen includes the two front languages as well.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this language arrangement help users?
teacher_understanding.answer: Displaying the denomination in multiple languages helps readers from different language backgrounds recognise the note's value.

prerequisites: front and reverse of a note
items.exam_note: Common distinction: 15 in the panel versus 17 in total.

terms.plain_meaning: note के एक हिस्से में कई भाषाओं में लिखा हुआ मूल्य
terms.everyday_image: एक ही कीमत को अलग-अलग भाषाओं में लिखी छोटी सूची

why_chain.step: Users read different languages.
The note displays its value through multiple languages, with the page counting 15 plus two.

unpack.example_or_place: Front: Hindi and English; reverse: 15-language panel.
unpack.consequence: Keep the panel count separate from the total count.
unpack.visual_verb: Flip the note and add 15 + 2 = 17.
unpack.level_extra: Do not confuse this count with the number of constitutionally scheduled languages.

items.content: Major security features:
Watermark of Mahatma Gandhi.

teacher_understanding.question: What watermark does the page identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies a watermark depicting Mahatma Gandhi as a major security feature.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is a watermark located?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is formed within the note paper, rather than being merely an ordinary surface-printed portrait.

teacher_understanding.question: How can it be examined?
teacher_understanding.answer: Holding the note against light reveals differences in light transmission that form the watermark image.

items.exam_note: Do not confuse the watermark with the ordinary printed portrait.

terms.plain_meaning: paper के अंदर बना हल्का चित्र जो रोशनी के सामने दिखता है
terms.everyday_image: note को बल्ब के सामने पकड़कर छिपा चेहरा देखना

why_chain.step: An ordinary printed copy can resemble a note's surface.
An image formed within the paper adds a different authentication check.

unpack.example_or_place: Mahatma Gandhi watermark on a note.
unpack.consequence: Use transmitted light, not just surface appearance.
unpack.visual_verb: Lift the note toward light and reveal the portrait.
unpack.level_extra: Features should be checked together, not as a single conclusive test.

items.content: Security Thread with "भारत", "RBI", and denomination.

teacher_understanding.question: What inscriptions does the security thread carry according to the page?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page lists “भारत”, “RBI”, and the denomination.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the security thread?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is incorporated into the note paper as a narrow security element.

teacher_understanding.question: How does checking the thread improve authentication?
teacher_understanding.answer: The user examines a specialised element and its lettering, rather than accepting any dark line drawn on paper as a genuine thread.

items.exam_note: Retain all three listed inscriptions; designs can vary.

terms.plain_meaning: note के paper में लगी सुरक्षा की पतली पट्टी
terms.everyday_image: कागज़ के बीच से जाती पतली line को पास से देखना

terms.plain_meaning: note पर लिखा रुपये का मूल्य

why_chain.step: A copied surface design may look convincing.
A specialised thread and its inscriptions offer an additional check.

unpack.example_or_place: Thread carrying “भारत”, “RBI” and denomination as listed.
unpack.consequence: Connect the physical thread with what is written on it.
unpack.visual_verb: Zoom into the thread and its lettering.
unpack.level_extra: A printed line alone is not equivalent to the security thread.

items.content: Latent Image visible when tilted.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the recognition cue for the latent image?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page says the image becomes visible when the note is tilted.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the user look for it?
teacher_understanding.answer: The user examines the designated latent-image area on the note while changing the viewing angle.

teacher_understanding.question: How is this different from a normal printed image?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its visibility depends on viewing angle, whereas ordinary print is generally readable without seeking that angle.

items.exam_note: Match latent image with tilting, not with a magnifying glass.

terms.plain_meaning: ऐसा छिपा चित्र जो खास angle से दिखे
terms.everyday_image: note झुकाते ही पहले छिपा निशान उभरना

why_chain.step: A flat copy may reproduce a visible design.
Angle-dependent visibility supplies a different checking action.

unpack.example_or_place: The latent-image feature on a note.
unpack.consequence: Teach tilt as a distinct action from holding against light.
unpack.visual_verb: Tilt the note until the image appears.
unpack.level_extra: Do not confuse image appearance with colour-changing ink.

items.content: See-through Register that forms the denomination when viewed against light.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the see-through register form?
teacher_understanding.answer: It forms the denomination when viewed against light.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are the complementary parts located?
teacher_understanding.answer: Parts of the design are printed in matching positions on the front and back of the note.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the complete number become visible?
teacher_understanding.answer: Transmitted light lets the viewer see the front and back portions together, so correctly aligned parts complete the numeral.

prerequisites: front and reverse of a note
items.exam_note: Match the register with front–back alignment against light.

terms.plain_meaning: आगे-पीछे छपे हिस्से जो रोशनी में मिलकर पूरा अंक बनाएँ
terms.everyday_image: दो अधूरे हिस्से मिलकर पूरा number बनाना

why_chain.step: A convincing note needs accurate printing on both sides.
The register tests whether the two parts align into the denomination.

unpack.example_or_place: The denomination completed when a note is held against light.
unpack.consequence: Distinguishes alignment checking from watermark recognition.
unpack.visual_verb: Overlay front and back fragments into one numeral.
unpack.level_extra: Watermark and register use light but are different features.

items.content: Micro-lettering reading "RBI" and the denomination.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the micro-lettering read?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page identifies the tiny lettering as “RBI” and the denomination.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is micro-lettering examined?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is examined in the small-print security areas of the note, rather than in the large value numerals.

teacher_understanding.question: How does it help authentication?
teacher_understanding.answer: Magnification can reveal whether the tiny lettering is formed clearly; ordinary copying may blur such fine detail.

items.exam_note: Link micro-lettering with tiny readable detail.

terms.plain_meaning: बहुत छोटे आकार में लिखे अक्षर और अंक
terms.everyday_image: magnifying glass से छोटे RBI अक्षर पढ़ना

why_chain.step: A counterfeit may reproduce large shapes but lose fine detail.
Tiny lettering adds a detail that can be checked closely.

unpack.example_or_place: “RBI” and denomination in the listed micro-lettering.
unpack.consequence: Adds a close-inspection check to light and tilt checks.
unpack.visual_verb: Magnify tiny print into readable letters.
unpack.level_extra: Do not confuse micro-lettering with larger accessibility numerals.

items.content: Optically Variable Ink on higher denominations.

teacher_understanding.question: What feature is listed for higher denominations?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page lists Optically Variable Ink.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the page place this feature?
teacher_understanding.answer: It associates the ink with higher-denomination notes without specifying particular values.

teacher_understanding.question: How does optically variable ink behave?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its apparent colour changes with viewing angle, supplying a visual check that ordinary single-colour printing does not provide.

items.exam_note: The page limits the claim to higher denominations; do not universalise it.

terms.plain_meaning: angle बदलने पर अलग रंग दिखाने वाली ink
terms.everyday_image: note झुकाते समय छपे हिस्से का रंग बदलता दिखना

why_chain.step: A static colour copy can imitate ordinary printing.
Angle-dependent colour adds a changing visual cue.

unpack.example_or_place: Higher denominations as stated on the page.
unpack.consequence: Tilt can test colour change as well as latent-image visibility.
unpack.visual_verb: Tilt and change the ink's apparent colour.
unpack.level_extra: Colour change and latent-image appearance are separate mechanisms.

items.content: Intaglio Printing (raised printing) for tactile feel.

teacher_understanding.question: What does intaglio printing provide here?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page describes it as raised printing that gives a tactile feel.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the effect felt?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is felt on the raised printed portions of the note surface.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this link security with accessibility?
teacher_understanding.answer: A user can feel relief rather than rely only on sight, providing a physical recognition cue that also assists users with impaired vision.

prerequisites: touch as a way of recognition
items.exam_note: Associate intaglio with raised tactile printing.

terms.plain_meaning: ऐसी printing जिससे छपा हिस्सा उभरा महसूस हो
terms.everyday_image: उँगली फेरने पर चिकने paper से अलग उभार महसूस करना

why_chain.step: Visual inspection alone is not equally useful to all users.
Raised printing supplies a tactile recognition cue.

unpack.example_or_place: Raised printed portions of a note.
unpack.consequence: Connects the security list back to accessibility features.
unpack.visual_verb: Run a fingertip across raised print.
unpack.level_extra: Avoid treating a flat printed imitation of a raised mark as equivalent.

items.content: Number Panels with increasing numeral size.

teacher_understanding.question: What pattern does the page identify in number panels?
teacher_understanding.answer: The numerals increase in size within the number panels.

teacher_understanding.question: Where should this pattern be checked?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is checked in the note's numbering panels, not by comparing the large denomination numerals on different notes.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this differ from a rise in monetary value?
teacher_understanding.answer: The change is in printed character size; it does not change the face value of the note.

items.exam_note: Increasing numeral size is not increasing denomination.

terms.plain_meaning: note पर उसका पहचान number छपा हुआ हिस्सा
terms.everyday_image: एक line में छोटे से बड़े होते छपे अंक

why_chain.step: Users need recognisable printing details to compare with an expected design.
The page supplies increasing numeral size as one such pattern.

unpack.example_or_place: Numbering panels on the note.
unpack.consequence: Completes the page's multi-feature security checklist.
unpack.visual_verb: Enlarge consecutive numerals along the panel.
unpack.level_extra: Keep serial numbering separate from denomination.

items.content: Promise on the Note

items.where_on_page: first bullet under Promise on the Note
items.content: It is known as the Promise Clause, and it signifies that the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) guarantees the face value of the note.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the promise clause signify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It signifies RBI's guarantee of the amount written as the note's face value.

teacher_understanding.question: Which kind of value is explicitly guaranteed on this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page specifies face value, rather than an inflation-adjusted value or a weight of precious metal.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is face value different from purchasing power?
teacher_understanding.answer: A ₹100 note remains denominated at ₹100 even if rising prices mean that ₹100 buys fewer goods.

items.exam_note: Nominal guarantee is not an inflation-protection or gold-redemption guarantee.

items.content: Bearer means that whoever physically possesses the note can use it.

teacher_understanding.question: Who is the bearer in this explanation?
teacher_understanding.answer: The bearer is the person physically holding the note and able to use it in payment.

teacher_understanding.question: What criterion identifies the bearer on this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: The criterion is physical possession, not a payee's name written on the note.

teacher_understanding.question: How does bearer use differ from a named bank account?
teacher_understanding.answer: A note can pass from hand to hand without changing a named account holder in bank records; an account balance is maintained against an identified account.

items.exam_note: Physical possession explains bearer use, not lawful ownership in every possible circumstance.

why_chain.step: Cash must pass between people without rewriting a payee's name.
Bearer use lets the physical holder use the note.

unpack.example_or_place: A note handed over at a shop.
unpack.consequence: Helps explain the later description of cash as anonymous.
unpack.visual_verb: Pass the note between hands.
unpack.level_extra: Possession and legal title should not be conflated.

items.content: Colonial era: Promised to convert into full bodied gold or silver bars / coins worth the equal value in weight.

teacher_understanding.question: To which period does the page attach metal convertibility?
teacher_understanding.answer: It attaches the promise of conversion into full-bodied gold or silver bars or coins to the colonial era.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does metal convertibility change the meaning of the promise?
teacher_understanding.answer: Under a convertible arrangement, the holder's claim is linked to specified metal redemption rather than simply the continued acceptance of a nominal currency amount.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the broad historical statement be handled carefully?
teacher_understanding.answer: Convertibility depended on the monetary system, period and eligible holder. This line should not be expanded into a claim that every colonial note was freely redeemable into either metal throughout colonial rule.

items.exam_note: Use the intended contrast with modern fiat currency, but avoid universal historical claims.

terms.plain_meaning: जिसमें metal की अपनी कीमत बताए गए मूल्य के बराबर हो
terms.everyday_image: ऐसा gold coin जिसकी कीमत उसके gold से आती हो

why_chain.step: People may seek a tangible asset behind a paper claim.
The page describes a historical promise to convert notes into gold or silver.

unpack.example_or_place: The page's colonial-era description of bars and coins.
unpack.consequence: Prepares the contrast with modern currency unlinked to metal weight.
unpack.visual_verb: Exchange a paper note for a metal bar or coin.
unpack.level_extra: Separate the book's broad contrast from precise period-specific convertibility rules.

items.content: Same was with the Dollar during the Bretton Woods System and the Pound Sterling during the British Rule.

teacher_understanding.question: Which historical settings does the page use as parallels?
teacher_understanding.answer: It names the Dollar during the Bretton Woods System and Pound Sterling during British Rule as parallels to metal-linked currency.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the book bring these currencies into the discussion?
teacher_understanding.answer: They illustrate its contrast between earlier metal-linked promises and modern currency not tied to a metal weight.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the Bretton Woods example be qualified?
teacher_understanding.answer: Dollar–gold convertibility under Bretton Woods was available to foreign official monetary holders, not a general right of every retail dollar holder. It therefore does not imply unrestricted public redemption of notes.

items.exam_note: Bretton Woods is an important linkage; avoid equating official convertibility with universal bearer redemption.

The page supplies the Dollar and Pound Sterling as parallels.

unpack.example_or_place: Dollar under Bretton Woods; Pound Sterling during British Rule.
unpack.consequence: Connects domestic currency promises with international monetary arrangements.
unpack.visual_verb: Place the two currencies on historical tracks beside metal.
unpack.level_extra: The page gives no precise dates or sterling redemption conditions.

The amount is partly obscured. Hindi text includes “मैं धारक को … रुपये अदा करने का वचन देता हूँ” and the guarantee wording “केन्द्रीय सरकार द्वारा प्रत्याभूत” below; part of the denomination is obscured.

teacher_understanding.answer: It shows the promise wording and Governor's signature area on a physical note.

teacher_understanding.question: Which visible wording connects it to the definitions above?
teacher_understanding.answer: “I PROMISE TO PAY THE BEARER” connects the image to both the promise clause and bearer.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the image be used without overreading it?
teacher_understanding.answer: Use the legible promise and role label as evidence; do not infer a precise denomination from the obscured amount.

items.exam_note: The Governor label in this illustration must not override the ₹1 note's Finance Secretary exception.

unpack.consequence: Anchors the abstract definitions in visible note wording.
unpack.visual_verb: Zoom into promise, bearer and signature.

items.content: Hindi promise and English “I PROMISE TO PAY THE BEARER THE SUM OF … HUNDRED RUPEES”: the printed payment promise, with the amount partly obscured.

teacher_understanding.question: What do these lines label?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are the promise printed on the illustrated note, in Hindi and English.

teacher_understanding.question: Which English word identifies the person addressed?
teacher_understanding.answer: The promise addresses the “BEARER”.

teacher_understanding.question: How does that wording connect to possession?
teacher_understanding.answer: It addresses the holder rather than naming a particular individual as payee.

items.exam_note: Recognise promise wording without inferring metal redemption.

unpack.consequence: Visual evidence for the promise-clause definition.
unpack.visual_verb: Underline “PROMISE” and “BEARER”.

items.content: “केन्द्रीय सरकार द्वारा प्रत्याभूत”: the Hindi guarantee wording below the promise area.

teacher_understanding.answer: The image includes Hindi wording stating a Central Government guarantee.

teacher_understanding.question: Which area of the image contains it?
teacher_understanding.answer: It appears below the Hindi promise, toward the lower left of the cropped note.

teacher_understanding.question: How should this be distinguished from the promise clause?
teacher_understanding.answer: The guarantee wording and the Governor's payment promise are related but separate printed elements; their presence should not be collapsed into one quotation.

items.exam_note: Keep the guarantee wording distinct from issuer and signatory facts.

teacher_understanding.answer: The visible label reads “GOVERNOR”.

teacher_understanding.question: Which separately discussed note has a different signatory?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page specifies the Finance Secretary of India as the signatory of the ₹1 note.

teacher_understanding.answer: The photograph illustrates a Governor-signed note; it does not mean that the ₹1 note carries the same signature.

items.content: Modern Currency:
Not inflation adjusted value. Not linked with weight of gold or silver.

teacher_understanding.question: How does modern currency differ from the earlier metal-linked description?
teacher_understanding.answer: The earlier description promises conversion into gold or silver; modern currency is described as not linked to a weight of either metal.

teacher_understanding.question: How is nominal face value different from inflation-adjusted value?
teacher_understanding.answer: Nominal value is the printed rupee amount. Inflation-adjusted value accounts for how much goods and services that amount can buy as prices change.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does a face-value guarantee not protect purchasing power?
teacher_understanding.answer: It preserves the stated monetary amount, not the prices of goods. If prices rise, the same amount buys less.

teacher_understanding.question: What two protections does the page say modern currency does not provide?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is not inflation adjusted and is not linked to a weight of gold or silver.

items.exam_note: Distinguish nominal value, real purchasing power and metal redemption.

terms.plain_meaning: महँगाई बदलने पर खरीदने की ताकत के हिसाब से बदली रकम
terms.everyday_image: पहले ₹100 में भरी थैली अब उसी ₹100 में आधी भरना

why_chain.step: Users care about both the rupee amount and what it buys.
The page limits modern currency's promise: no inflation adjustment and no gold or silver weight link.

unpack.example_or_place: A ₹100 note whose printed value stays ₹100 while shopping prices change.
unpack.consequence: Trust in currency does not imply a fixed real value.
unpack.visual_verb: Keep ₹100 fixed while the goods basket shrinks; disconnect a gold-weight link.
unpack.level_extra: No metal-redemption link does not mean that an issuing institution holds no gold assets.

items.content: Currency note is zero interest, anonymous bearer bond.

teacher_understanding.question: Which three attributes does the book attach to the note?
teacher_understanding.answer: It describes a currency note as zero interest, anonymous and bearer, using the expression “bearer bond”.

teacher_understanding.question: Which earlier definition supports the bearer attribute?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page has already defined bearer as the person who physically possesses the note and can use it.

teacher_understanding.question: How should zero interest and anonymous be understood?
teacher_understanding.answer: Holding a cash note does not itself earn interest, and the note is not registered in the holder's name. This does not mean that every cash transaction is untraceable.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should the word bond be treated cautiously?
teacher_understanding.answer: Here it is an economic shorthand for an issuer-backed bearer claim, not a reason to classify ordinary currency as a conventional investment bond with maturity and redemption terms.

items.exam_note: Open each adjective separately; do not infer legal promissory-note or conventional bond status.
